s723.content:
Born into a noble Venetian family, Lawrence joined the canons of San Giorgio in Alga at nineteen and later became their superior. In 1433 he was made bishop of Castello, and in 1451 Pope Nicholas V made him the first Patriarch of Venice.

He lived poorly, gave generously to the poor, and wrote spiritual works. He was canonized in 1690, and the 1962 calendar keeps his feast on September 5.
s723.intercession: St. Lawrence Justinian, pray for us, and for the people of Venice. Amen.

s724.content:
Gorgonius was an officer of the imperial household at Nicomedia who was martyred with Dorotheus and Peter in the persecution of Diocletian, in 304.

His relics were brought to Rome and later to the abbey of Gorze in Lorraine, which spread his cult in the West. The 1962 calendar commemorates him on September 9.
s724.intercession: St. Gorgonius, pray for us, and for all who serve in high places. Amen.

s725.content:
Protus and Hyacinth were martyrs of the persecution of Valerian, honored on this day in the earliest Roman calendar, the Depositio Martyrum of 354.

In 1845 the unopened tomb of Hyacinth was found in the Catacomb of Basilla on the Via Salaria, with his name inscribed and his remains inside. The 1962 calendar commemorates them on September 11.
s725.intercession: Sts. Protus and Hyacinth, pray for us. Amen.

s726.content:
Linus was the first successor of St. Peter as bishop of Rome. St. Irenaeus identifies him with the Linus who sends greetings in St. Paul’s Second Letter to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21).

He is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass, just after the apostles. The 1962 calendar keeps his feast on September 23.
s726.intercession: St. Linus, pray for us, and for the successor of St. Peter. Amen.

s727.content:
According to their legend, Cyprian was a pagan sorcerer of Antioch who tried by magic to lead astray a Christian virgin, Justina. Her prayers and the Sign of the Cross defeated his spells, and he was converted, became a Christian, and in the story a bishop. Both were martyred at Nicomedia about 304.

The story is legendary, and this Cyprian is not St. Cyprian of Carthage. The 1962 calendar commemorates them on September 26.
s727.intercession: Sts. Cyprian and Justina, pray for us. Defend us against every evil. Amen.

s728.content:
Placid was entrusted as a boy to St. Benedict at Subiaco. St. Gregory the Great tells how he was saved from drowning in a lake when St. Maurus, sent by Benedict, ran across the water to pull him out.

A later legend made him the founder of a monastery in Sicily, martyred there by pirates with his brothers and sister; that story is not historical. The 1962 calendar commemorates him with his companions on October 5.
s728.intercession: St. Placid, pray for us, and for all young people seeking God. Amen.

s729.content:
Chrysanthus and Daria were Roman martyrs, named in the early lists and buried on the Via Salaria, where a church was built over their grave.

Their legend makes Chrysanthus the son of a nobleman from Alexandria and Daria a pagan woman of Rome whom he converted and married, and says that they were buried alive. The 1962 calendar commemorates them on October 25.
s729.intercession: Sts. Chrysanthus and Daria, pray for us, and for all married couples. Amen.

s730.content:
Evaristus was the fourth successor of St. Peter as bishop of Rome, from about 99 to 107. Little is known of him. The apostle John probably died in his time, closing the age of the apostles.

The Liber Pontificalis says that he divided Rome among its priests, the beginning of its parishes. The 1962 calendar commemorates him on October 26.
s730.intercession: St. Evaristus, pray for us, and for every parish. Amen.

s731.content:
Born Lancelot Avellino in the kingdom of Naples, he became a priest and a church lawyer. After a lie told in court troubled his conscience, he left the law to serve souls. When he was attacked for reforming a convent of nuns, he joined the Theatines in 1556, taking the name Andrew. He was a tireless confessor and spiritual director, and a friend of St. Charles Borromeo.

In 1608 he collapsed at the foot of the altar as he began Mass, and died the same day; he is invoked against sudden death. The 1962 calendar keeps his feast on November 10.
s731.intercession: St. Andrew Avellino, pray for us, now and at the hour of our death. Amen.

s732.content:
Felix was a hermit at Cerfroid near Meaux in France who, with St. John of Matha, founded the Order of the Most Holy Trinity in 1198 to ransom Christians held captive.

Tradition made him a member of the French royal house of Valois, but this and much else about his life is uncertain, and in 1969 his feast was removed from the general calendar. The 1962 calendar keeps it on November 20.
s732.intercession: St. Felix, pray for us, and for all who are held captive. Amen.

s733.content:
A canon of Osimo in Italy, Sylvester was moved to leave the world when he looked into the open grave of a once handsome friend. He became a hermit at Montefano near Fabriano, where disciples gathered around him, and founded the Sylvestrine Benedictines, approved by Pope Innocent IV in 1248.

He died in 1267 at about ninety. The 1962 calendar keeps his feast on November 26.
s733.intercession: St. Sylvester, pray for us. Teach us to remember our end and live for God. Amen.

s734.content:
Saturninus, called Sernin in France, was sent from Rome in the third century to preach the Gospel in Gaul and became the first bishop of Toulouse. He was martyred about 257: refusing to sacrifice to the gods, he was tied to a bull and dragged to his death.

The great Romanesque Basilica of Saint-Sernin in Toulouse stands over his tomb. The 1962 calendar commemorates him on November 29.
s734.intercession: St. Saturninus, pray for us, and for all who bring the Gospel to new lands. Amen.

s735.content:
Bibiana was a Roman virgin and martyr. In the fifth century Pope Simplicius consecrated a basilica in her honor over her body; it was rebuilt in the 1620s by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, his first work of architecture, with his statue of the saint over the altar.

Her legend places her martyrdom under Julian the Apostate in the 360s. The 1962 calendar keeps her feast on December 2.
s735.intercession: St. Bibiana, pray for us. Make us faithful and pure of heart. Amen.

s736.content:
Melchiades, or Miltiades, an African by birth, was bishop of Rome from 311 to 314, when the persecutions ended and the emperor Constantine granted Christians freedom.

He received from the emperor the Lateran palace, which became the residence of the popes, and in 313 he presided over a council at the Lateran that judged the Donatist dispute in Africa. The 1962 calendar commemorates him on December 10.
s736.intercession: St. Melchiades, pray for us, and for peace in the Church. Amen.

s737.content:
John of Ávila was a priest of Andalusia who hoped to sail as a missionary to the Americas, but the archbishop of Seville kept him at home to preach in southern Spain. Accused before the Inquisition, he spent about a year in prison, where he began his book Audi, filia, and was cleared.

His preaching brought about the conversion of St. John of God, and he guided St. Teresa of Ávila and St. Francis Borgia. Canonized in 1970, he was named a Doctor of the Church in 2012.
s737.intercession: St. John of Ávila, pray for us, and for all priests. Amen.

s738.content:
Gregory Palamas left the imperial court of Constantinople as a young man to become a monk on Mount Athos, where he learned the Jesus Prayer and the stillness of hesychasm. When the scholar Barlaam of Calabria mocked the monks’ prayer, Gregory defended it, teaching that God, unknowable in his essence, truly gives himself to us in his uncreated energies.

Councils in Constantinople upheld his teaching, and he became archbishop of Thessalonica. The Byzantine churches keep his memory on November 14 and on the Second Sunday of the Great Fast.
s738.intercession: Holy Father Gregory, pray for us, that we may come to know God in prayer. Amen.

s739.content:
In the 1230s seven cloth merchants of Florence, members of a confraternity devoted to the Blessed Virgin, left their trade to live together in prayer and penance, at last on Monte Senario outside the city.

From their life grew the Order of Servants of Mary, the Servites, devoted to Our Lady of Sorrows. The last of them, Alexis Falconieri, died in 1310. Leo XIII canonized all seven together in 1888. The 1962 calendar keeps their feast on February 12.
s739.intercession: Holy Seven Founders, pray for us, and teach us to serve Mary. Amen.

s740.content:
Willibald, an Anglo-Saxon from Wessex, made a long pilgrimage to Rome and the Holy Land in the 720s, one of the earliest such journeys recorded by an Englishman, and then lived for ten years as a monk at Monte Cassino, helping to restore it.

Pope Gregory III sent him to help his kinsman St. Boniface in Germany, and Boniface made him the first bishop of Eichstätt in Bavaria. His sister was St. Walburga.
s740.intercession: St. Willibald, pray for us, pilgrims on the way to our true home. Amen.

s741.content:
Kilian was an Irish monk and bishop who traveled with companions to Franconia, in what is now Germany, and preached the Gospel at Würzburg, where the local duke Gosbert was baptized.

According to the old account, he told the duke that his marriage to his brother’s widow, Geilana, was unlawful, and while the duke was away Geilana had Kilian and his companions Colman and Totnan killed, about 689.
s741.intercession: St. Kilian, pray for us. Give us courage to speak the truth with love. Amen.

s742.content:
Adelaide, a princess of Burgundy, was married young to King Lothair of Italy and widowed at nineteen. Imprisoned by Lothair’s rival Berengar, she escaped and married the German king Otto the Great, and in 962 she was crowned empress with him in Rome.

As a widow she governed for a time for her grandson Otto III, then gave herself to prayer and to founding churches and monasteries, encouraged by St. Odilo of Cluny. She died at the convent she had founded at Selz in Alsace in 999.
s742.intercession: St. Adelaide, pray for us, and for all who suffer in their families. Amen.

s743.content:
Ludger, a Frisian born near Utrecht, studied at York under Alcuin before returning as a priest and missionary among the Frisians and Saxons. When Saxon uprisings drove him out, he went to Rome and Monte Cassino, then came back at Charlemagne’s request.

He founded the abbey of Werden and became the first bishop of Münster, a city named for the monastery he built there. He died in 809 at Billerbeck while visiting his diocese.
s743.intercession: St. Ludger, pray for us, and for all who carry the Gospel to others. Amen.

s744.content:
Afra was a Christian of Augsburg martyred in the persecution of Diocletian, burned on an island in the river Lech. Her tomb was honored from early times, and the poet Venantius Fortunatus mentions it in the sixth century.

A later legend tells that she had been a prostitute, converted by a bishop who sheltered in her house, and she became a patron of penitents. The basilica of Sts. Ulrich and Afra in Augsburg keeps her memory.
s744.intercession: St. Afra, pray for us, and for all who turn back to God. Amen.

s745.content:
Meinrad was a monk of Reichenau who left to live as a hermit in the dark forest of Switzerland, where he kept a small chapel with an image of Our Lady. Pilgrims came to him for prayer and counsel, and he received them all as guests.

In 861 two robbers he had welcomed and fed killed him, hoping to find treasure. Ravens that he had fed were said to follow the murderers and betray them. On the site of his cell grew the Abbey of Einsiedeln.
s745.intercession: St. Meinrad, pray for us. Make us welcoming to every guest. Amen.

s746.content:
Bernward was a tutor of the young emperor Otto III before becoming bishop of Hildesheim in 993. He defended his city against raiders, built walls, and was himself skilled in metalwork and painting.

He founded the abbey church of St. Michael at Hildesheim and commissioned the great bronze doors, now in Hildesheim Cathedral, and a bronze column showing the life of Christ, still among the finest works of their age. He died a monk of his own abbey in 1022 and was canonized in 1192.
s746.intercession: St. Bernward, pray for us, and for all who make beautiful things for God. Amen.

s747.content:
Anna Schäffer of Mindelstetten in Bavaria wanted to be a missionary sister, but at nineteen, working as a maid, she fell into a vat of boiling lye and scalded both legs. The wounds never healed, and she spent the rest of her life bedridden in pain.

At first bitter, she came to see her bed as a place of prayer, offering her suffering for others, and she wrote letters of comfort to the many who sought her out. Benedict XVI canonized her in 2012.
s747.intercession: St. Anna Schäffer, pray for us, and for all who suffer long illness. Amen.

s748.content:
Bernhard Lichtenberg was provost of St. Hedwig’s Cathedral in Berlin. After the pogrom of November 1938, he prayed publicly every evening for the persecuted Jews and for the prisoners in the concentration camps.

Arrested in 1941, he was sentenced to prison and, when his term ended, sent toward Dachau, but he died on the way, at Hof in Bavaria, on November 5, 1943. John Paul II beatified him in Berlin in 1996.
s748.intercession: Blessed Bernhard, pray for us. Give us courage to pray and speak for the persecuted. Amen.

s749.content:
Karl Leisner, a youth leader from Kleve in the Rhineland, was a deacon when he was arrested in 1939 for a remark about Hitler and sent at last to Dachau, where he fell ill with tuberculosis.

On December 17, 1944, a French bishop who was also a prisoner secretly ordained him a priest in the camp, and he celebrated his only Mass days later. Freed in 1945, he died of his illness on August 12 that year. John Paul II beatified him in 1996.
s749.intercession: Blessed Karl, pray for us, and for young people who seek God. Amen.

s750.content:
Józef Bilczewski, a peasant’s son from Wilamowice in southern Poland, became a professor of theology at Lviv and in 1900 the Latin-rite archbishop of the city. He built churches and schools in its poor districts, and through the First World War and the fighting that followed he cared for the hungry, the wounded, and refugees of every nation.

He asked to be buried among the poor in the city’s Janów cemetery. Benedict XVI canonized him in 2005.
s750.intercession: St. Józef Bilczewski, pray for us, and for peace among the nations. Amen.

s751.content:
In 1619, during the Thirty Years’ War, troops of the Transylvanian prince Gabriel Bethlen took the city of Košice. Three Catholic priests there, the Croatian canon Marko Krizin and the Jesuits Melchior Grodziecki, a Pole, and Stephen Pongrácz, a Hungarian, were seized, tortured, and pressed to renounce their faith.

They refused and were killed on September 7. John Paul II canonized them in Košice in 1995.
s751.intercession: Holy Martyrs of Košice, pray for us, and for the unity of Christians. Amen.

s752.content:
John, from the town of Dukla in the Carpathian foothills of Poland, lived for a time as a hermit before joining the Conventual Franciscans, and served as guardian of friaries in Krosno and Lviv. Late in life he joined the stricter Observant Franciscans, the Bernardines, in Lviv.

There he preached and heard confessions tirelessly, even after he went blind. He died in Lviv in 1484, and John Paul II canonized him in Krosno in 1997.
s752.intercession: St. John of Dukla, pray for us. Make us faithful to the end. Amen.

s753.content:
Simon studied at the University of Kraków and joined the Bernardines, the Observant Franciscans, drawn by the preaching of St. John of Capistrano. He became a famed preacher in Kraków, devoted to the Holy Name of Jesus.

When plague struck the city in 1482, he nursed the sick until he caught it himself and died. Benedict XVI canonized him in 2007.
s753.intercession: St. Simon of Lipnica, pray for us, and for all who care for the sick. Amen.

s754.content:
Edmund Rich of Abingdon taught at Paris and Oxford, among the first to lecture there on Aristotle, and was known for his prayer and his poverty. In 1233 he was chosen archbishop of Canterbury.

He worked to reform the clergy and stood up to King Henry III over the rights of the Church, and at last he set out for Rome. He died on the way at Soisy in France in 1240 and was buried at the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny. He was canonized in 1246.
s754.intercession: St. Edmund, pray for us, and for all students and teachers. Amen.

s755.content:
According to her medieval Life, Winefride was a young Welsh noblewoman who resolved to give herself to God. When a chieftain named Caradog tried to force himself on her, she fled toward the church, and he struck off her head. Where it fell a spring burst forth, and her uncle, St. Beuno, raised her to life.

She lived on as a nun and abbess. St. Winefride’s Well at Holywell in north Wales has drawn pilgrims since the Middle Ages, even through the Reformation.
s755.intercession: St. Winefride, pray for us, and for all who seek healing. Amen.

s756.content:
Ita founded a small community of women at Killeedy in County Limerick and became one of the best-loved saints of Ireland, called the foster mother of the saints of Erin. Tradition says that St. Brendan the Navigator was in her care as a child.

Asked what God loves most, she is said to have answered: true faith in God with a pure heart, a simple life with piety, and generosity inspired by charity.
s756.intercession: St. Ita, pray for us, and for all who raise children in the faith. Amen.

s757.content:
Ciarán, a carpenter’s son, studied under St. Finnian of Clonard and then founded a monastery at Clonmacnoise, beside the river Shannon, in about 545. He died young, within a year of the founding, perhaps of the plague.

Clonmacnoise grew into one of the greatest monasteries and schools of Ireland, and its high crosses and round tower still stand.
s757.intercession: St. Ciarán, pray for us. Teach us to build what will outlast us. Amen.

s758.content:
Benedict Biscop, a Northumbrian nobleman, gave up the king’s service to become a monk and made several journeys to Rome. He founded the twin monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow in the north of England.

From Rome and Gaul he brought back books, paintings, glaziers, and masons, and even John, the archcantor of St. Peter’s, to teach Roman chant. The library he gathered formed his pupil St. Bede the Venerable.
s758.intercession: St. Benedict Biscop, pray for us, and for all who love learning and beauty. Amen.

s759.content:
Ivo Hélory studied law at Paris and Orléans and served as a church judge in Brittany, where he became known for his honesty and for defending the poor without charge. Ordained a priest, he gave up his legal posts to serve as a parish priest.

He turned his family house into a shelter for the poor and lived simply among them. An old Latin verse praised him as a lawyer who was not a thief, a thing for the people to marvel at.
s759.intercession: St. Ivo, pray for us, and for all who work for justice. Amen.

s760.content:
John Francis Regis was a Jesuit who spent his priesthood preaching missions in the rugged mountains of the Vivarais and Velay in southern France, walking from village to village even in deep winter to teach the faith and hear confessions.

He opened refuges for women leaving prostitution and helped the poor lacemakers of Le Puy find work. Worn out, he died while preaching a mission at La Louvesc on December 31, 1640. He was canonized in 1737.
s760.intercession: St. John Francis Regis, pray for us, and for all who are forgotten. Amen.

s761.content:
Nuno Álvares Pereira was the constable of Portugal who led its armies to victory at Aljubarrota in 1385, securing the kingdom’s independence. Even as a soldier he was known for his prayer, his devotion to Our Lady, and his mercy to the defeated.

After his wife died, he gave away his wealth and entered the Carmelite friary he had founded in Lisbon, taking the name Nuno of St. Mary and living as a humble brother who begged for the poor. Benedict XVI canonized him in 2009.
s761.intercession: St. Nuno, pray for us, and for all who serve as soldiers. Amen.

s762.content:
Alexandrina Maria da Costa of Balasar in northern Portugal was fourteen when she leapt from a window to escape men who broke into her home. The fall injured her spine, and from 1925 she was paralyzed and bedridden for the rest of her life.

She offered her sufferings for sinners and for love of the Eucharist, and asked for the consecration of the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary, which Pius XII made in 1942. For her last thirteen years, it was reported, she took no food but Holy Communion. John Paul II beatified her in 2004.
s762.intercession: Blessed Alexandrina, pray for us, and for all who cannot leave their beds. Amen.
